body.en:
A rate rise warning amid a strong jobs market, super news for retirees despite a property downturn, and records broken for Australia’s avocado industry.

SBS Finance Editor Ricardo Gonçalves takes a look at three finance news stories of the week and explains how they’ll impact you.

Superannuation funds have delivered another standout year for Australians, but experts say investors shouldn't expect these returns to continue.

Australia's jobs market remains stronger than expected, fuelling speculation the Reserve Bank could raise interest rates again, and avocado lovers have been given some welcome news with prices tipped to stay low.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Australia's superannuation funds have delivered another impressive year, but experts are warning members not to expect these returns every year.

New data from superannuation research firm Chant West shows the median growth fund returned 9.5 per cent over the past financial year, marking four consecutive years of returns above 9 per cent.

Chant West head of superannuation investment Mano Mohankumar told the SBS On the Money podcast that while recent performance has been strong, it's unlikely to continue indefinitely.

Strong international sharemarket gains helped drive returns, with global shares rising more than 25 per cent over the year. Australian shares also posted solid gains of around 6 per cent.

One of the few weaker spots was Australian listed property, which comes as new figures from Domain showed national median house and unit prices recorded their first quarterly decline in more than three years.

The chance of another interest rate rise increased this week after stronger-than-expected employment figures.

More than 76,000 jobs were created last month, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.4 per cent because more Australians entered the workforce, pushing the participation rate to a one-year high of 67 per cent.

The participation rate measures the share of working-age Australians who are either employed or actively looking for work. Economists say the increase could reflect ongoing demand for workers or more people seeking employment as cost of living pressures persist.

Citi Australia senior economist Faraz Syed told the SBS On the Money podcast the key concern for the Reserve Bank is whether a tight labour market starts driving wages significantly higher.

The next official inflation figures will be released on Wednesday, ahead of the Reserve Bank's next board meeting on 10 August.

title.en: Police confirm abusive phone call to synagogue not logged, at antisemitism royal commission
title.zh: 警方证实反犹太主义皇家委员会未记录对犹太教堂的辱骂电话

summary.en: Police, security and funding concerns dominated the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion this weke.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及公义、尊严与问责。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
The relationship between police and Jewish community security groups came under scrutiny as the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion wrapped up its fifth hearing block in Melbourne.

Across five days, the inquiry heard evidence about the growing financial burden of security for Jewish Australians, police responses to antisemitic incidents, media coverage of the Hamas-Israel war and preparations for future hearings into last year's Bondi terror attack.

Today's hearings focused on the relationship between police and Jewish community security organisations, with Liberal MP Julian Leeser, Dor Foundation chief executive Tahli Blicblau, AFP assistant commissioner Stephen Nutt and Victoria Police assistant commissioner Martin O'Brien among those appearing before the commission.

The evidence is expected to help shape the commission's understanding of police data collection, security risk assessments and the role of emergency preparedness in responding to threats against the Jewish community.

Victoria Police also faced scrutiny over how antisemitic incidents are recorded. The commission heard an abusive phone call to a synagogue, in which the congregation was allegedly described as "genocidal" and "maggot rat Jews", was not recorded as a prejudice-motivated incident.

O'Brien confirmed no incident fact sheet had been logged for the call, which is required for any prejudice-motivated crime that relates to racial, political or ideological circumstances.

O'Brien said the force had "automatic scanning" every day of incidents, along with human analysts to consider threats.

A separate incident involving a 5.5m Nazi hakenkreuz symbol painted on a construction site was also not categorised under the relevant reporting system.

Security funding emerged as one of the dominant themes of the week's hearings, with Jewish community leaders telling the commission families, schools, places of worship and community organisations continue to bear much of the cost of keeping their communities safe.

On Thursday, the commission heard government funding since 2023 has covered about half of the security costs incurred by the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, which received $25 million to distribute to community organisations, places of worship and events.

Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim told the inquiry governments should ideally reimburse the council for all security costs it handles, while almost 200 organisations have applied for the latest federal funding allocation of $124 million over three years.

body.en:
Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine, after police stopped him while speeding over a bridge.

The 22-year-old, who represented Australia at the World Cup , was caught speeding twice overnight, NSW Police said on Friday.

Driving a BMW, Volpato was allegedly clocked at 109 km/h — nearly 50 km/h over the designated speed limit — when police stopped him on Sydney's Anzac Bridge at 1.10am on Friday.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine, police said in a statement.

Volpato had earlier been stopped at 11.05pm on Thursday, police said, for travelling between 86 and 94km/h in a 60 zone.

Volpato returned a negative result when he was given the initial roadside breath test.

Volpato, who plays club football for Italian side Sassuolo, made three appearances for the Socceroos at the World Cup.

He made headlines shortly before the tournament when he switched his international allegiance from Italy to Australia.

Volpato, who was born and raised in Sydney and played his junior football at Sydney United 58, Sydney FC and Western Sydney before moving overseas, represented Italy at U19 and U20 level.

The 22-year-old, who has scored seven goals in his three seasons with Sassuolo after two seasons with fellow Serie A club Roma, said in March he was "waiting for Italy" to select him for the senior side, who subsequently failed to qualify for the World Cup.

body.en:
Deadly H5 bird flu appears to have reached Queensland's coastline for the first time as detections in wild seabirds across Australia climb to 17, sparking fresh warnings for vulnerable wildlife.

A deceased petrel found on Moreton Island returned an initial positive result for highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza at the Queensland government's Biosecurity Sciences Laboratory.

Samples have been sent to CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness for confirmatory testing.

Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said the arrival of H5 bird flu in Queensland should alarm anybody concerned about Australia's native animals.

"Bird flu has now reached Queensland's coastline, and that should concern every Australian who cares about our wildlife," Booth said.

"We can't stop this virus, but we can boost the capacity of wildlife to survive and recover from outbreaks."

Australia reported its first case of H5 bird flu on 20 June, and there are now 17 confirmed detections of the serious H5 strain in wild seabirds — 10 in Western Australia, five in South Australia and two in NSW.

Booth said surveillance efforts were working but warned they would not be enough once the virus hit vulnerable species.

"Finding cases is only the first step — once this disease reaches vulnerable wildlife populations, surveillance won't prevent the devastating impacts we've seen overseas," she said.

"Millions of wild birds and marine mammals have died, and unless we do everything we can to strengthen the resilience of at-risk populations, there's every reason to fear Australia could face similar losses."

There have been no detections in poultry and no evidence of large-scale deaths in any animals in Queensland, according to the Department of Primary Industries.

"It is safe to continue to eat chicken meat or eggs, and I would encourage Queenslanders to purchase these products as they normally would," said Queensland's Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett.

Queensland's Chief Veterinary Officer, Allison Crook, said the suspected positive result was anticipated and the state was well prepared.

"We have known that a H5 bird flu detection in Queensland was a matter of when, not if," Crook said.

"This suspect positive result has not impacted our poultry sector or native wildlife and we are continuing our enhanced passive surveillance program throughout the state and would encourage the community and industry to continue to be vigilant."

Booth continued to urge the federal government to back a major "wildlife resilience" package to help species withstand bird flu and other threats.
